text: (1) The Central Government shall constitute the National Occupational Safety and Health Advisory Board to advise it on standards, rules and regulations, implementation issues, and policy matters relating to occupational safety and health.

sub_structure.2: (2) The National Board's membership includes senior officials such as the Secretary of Labour and Employment (Chairperson), Directors General of Factory Advice/Mines Safety/Health Services, State Principal Secretaries, and equal representation (five each) of employers and employees.
sub_structure.3: (3) Members representing States, employers, employees and professional bodies serve three-year terms.
sub_structure.5: (5) The Central Government may constitute technical or advisory committees to assist the National Board.

plain_english_summary: A national tripartite body — government officials plus equal numbers of employer and worker representatives — is set up to advise the Centre on workplace safety standards and policy.

title: State Occupational Safety and Health Advisory Board
text: (1) Each State Government shall constitute a State Occupational Safety and Health Advisory Board to advise it on matters arising from administering this Code as referred to it.

sub_structure.3: (3) The State Government may constitute technical, advisory or site appraisal committees to assist the State Advisory Board within its jurisdiction.

plain_english_summary: Every State gets its own advisory safety board mirroring the National Board, to advise the State Government on OSH matters within its jurisdiction.

title: Occupational safety and health standards
text: (1) The Central Government shall declare, by notification, standards on occupational safety and health for workplaces relating to factories, mines, dock work, beedi and cigar, building/construction work and other establishments.

sub_structure.2: (2) These standards must cover hazard exposure limits, hazard-appraisal norms, monitoring/measurement of exposure, medical examinations at employer's cost, and hazard evaluation procedures like safety audits.
sub_structure.2_f: (f) matters specified in the Second Schedule to the Code.
sub_structure.3: (3) The Central Government may amend the Second Schedule by notification, after giving 45 days' notice, based on the National Board's recommendation.
sub_structure.4: (4) A State Government may, with prior Central Government approval, amend the standards for establishments within its jurisdiction.

plain_english_summary: The Central Government sets the actual technical safety standards — hazard limits, monitoring requirements, mandatory medical checks — that establishments across industries must follow.

title: Research related activities
text: It shall be the duty of institutions notified by the Central or State Government in the field of occupational safety and health to conduct research, experiments and demonstrations relating to occupational safety and health, and submit recommendations to the Government.

sub_structure.proviso: Provided that a State Government must consult the National Board before notifying such research, experiments or demonstrations.

plain_english_summary: Designated research institutions are tasked with studying occupational safety and health issues and feeding recommendations back to government, with States required to loop in the National Board first.

title: Safety and occupational health surveys
text: (1) At any time during normal working hours (or otherwise as necessary), designated officers (Chief Inspector-cum-Facilitator, Director General of Factory Advice Service, Director General of Mines Safety, Director General of Health Services, or another authorised officer) may, after written notice, conduct a safety/health survey of a factory, mine or other establishment, and the employer must provide all facilities for it.

sub_structure.2: (2) Workers must, if required by the survey officer, undergo medical examination and furnish relevant information.
sub_structure.3: (3) Time spent by a worker undergoing such examination or furnishing information counts as working hours for wage/overtime purposes.

plain_english_summary: Government safety officers can conduct on-site safety and health surveys of workplaces, and employers/workers must cooperate fully — with workers' survey participation time counted and paid as regular working hours.

title: Collection of statistics and portal for inter-State migrant workers
text: (1) The Central and State Governments shall collect, compile and analyse occupational safety and health statistics in the prescribed form and manner.

sub_structure.2: (2) The Governments shall maintain an electronic database/portal for inter-State migrant workers; a migrant worker may self-register on the portal using self-declaration and Aadhaar, and self-employed workers who have migrated may also register.

plain_english_summary: The government must maintain nationwide OSH statistics, and separately run a dedicated portal where inter-State migrant workers (including self-employed migrants) can self-register using Aadhaar to be officially tracked and reached with benefits.

title: Safety Committee and safety officers
text: (1) The appropriate Government may require any establishment or class of establishments to constitute a Safety Committee with employer and worker representatives, where worker representatives must be at least as numerous as employer representatives.

sub_structure.2: (2) Establishments crossing certain worker thresholds — factories with 500+ workers (250+ for hazardous processes), construction sites with 250+ workers, or mines with 100+ workers — must additionally appoint qualified safety officers.

plain_english_summary: Larger and higher-risk workplaces must set up a joint employer-worker Safety Committee (with workers holding at least equal representation) and appoint dedicated, qualified safety officers once they cross specific worker-count thresholds.

title: Responsibility of employer for maintaining health, safety and working conditions
text: (1) The employer shall be responsible to maintain in his establishment such health, safety and working conditions for employees as may be prescribed by the Central Government.

sub_structure.2: (2) These may include cleanliness/hygiene, ventilation/temperature/humidity, dust and fume-free environments, potable drinking water, anti-overcrowding space standards, adequate lighting, separate latrine/urinal facilities for male/female/transgender employees, and effluent/waste treatment arrangements.

plain_english_summary: Employers must maintain baseline physical working conditions — clean air, adequate lighting and space, drinking water, and gender-inclusive sanitation facilities — as detailed by Central Government rules.

title: Welfare facilities in the establishment, etc.
text: (1) The employer shall provide prescribed welfare facilities including separate washing and bathing facilities for male/female/transgender employees, storage for personal clothing, sitting arrangements, canteens (where 100+ workers are employed), pre-employment mine medical exams, and accessible first-aid boxes.

sub_structure.2_i: (2)(i) Ambulance rooms are required in factories, mines or construction sites with more than 500 workers.
sub_structure.2_iv: (iv) A welfare officer must be appointed in factories, mines or plantations with 250 or more workers.
sub_structure.2_v: (v) Employers must provide free temporary living accommodation at or near the worksite for building workers.
sub_structure.3: (3) The Central Government may require creche facilities (for children under six) in establishments with more than 50 workers, which can be run jointly/pooled with other establishments or government/NGO facilities.

plain_english_summary: Beyond bare safety, employers must fund tangible welfare amenities — separate washrooms, canteens, first-aid, on-site housing for construction workers, and creches for young children — scaled to the size of the establishment.

chapter_title: HOURS OF WORK AND ANNUAL LEAVE WITH WAGES
title: Daily and weekly working hours, leave, etc.
text: (1) No worker shall be required or allowed to work in any establishment for more than eight hours in a day, with specific rules for underground mine shifts and motor transport workers' running/subsidiary time.

sub_structure.2: (2) Working journalists are capped at 144 hours over any 4 consecutive weeks, with at least 24 consecutive hours of rest in any 7-day period.
sub_structure.3: (3) Sales promotion employees and working journalists get earned leave (at least 1/11th of days on duty) and half-pay medical leave, with cash compensation for unused earned leave on resignation, termination or death.
sub_structure.4: (4) Adolescent workers' hours are governed instead by the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986.

plain_english_summary: The standard workday is capped at eight hours, with special hour limits for mine, transport and journalism work, and journalists/sales staff get guaranteed leave entitlements including cash-out of unused leave.

chapter_title: HOURS OF WORK AND ANNUAL LEAVE WITH WAGES
title: Weekly and compensatory holidays
text: (1) No worker shall work more than six days in any one week, though motor transport employers may adjust holiday days to avoid service disruption, provided no worker works more than 10 consecutive days without a full holiday.

sub_structure.3: (3) Workers deprived of a weekly holiday due to an exemption order must be given a compensatory holiday within the same month or the following two months.

plain_english_summary: Workers are guaranteed at least one rest day per week (max six working days), and if that holiday is skipped for operational reasons, it must be made up soon after.

chapter_title: HOURS OF WORK AND ANNUAL LEAVE WITH WAGES
title: Extra wages for overtime
text: Workers who work beyond the prescribed daily/weekly hours are entitled to overtime wages at twice the normal rate, calculated whichever way (daily or weekly) is more favourable to the worker, and overtime requires the worker's consent.
plain_english_summary: Overtime must be paid at double the normal wage rate, and — importantly — a worker cannot be forced into overtime without their consent.

chapter_title: HOURS OF WORK AND ANNUAL LEAVE WITH WAGES
title: Night shifts
text: Where a worker's shift extends past midnight, the weekly holiday for that worker is counted as a 24-hour period starting when the shift ends, and hours worked after midnight are attributed to the previous day for record purposes.
plain_english_summary: A technical but practical rule: for night-shift workers, 'the day' and 'the weekly holiday' are measured from when their shift actually ends, not the calendar clock, so their rest entitlements aren't shortchanged.

chapter_title: HOURS OF WORK AND ANNUAL LEAVE WITH WAGES
title: Prohibition of overlapping shifts
text: (1) Work shall not be organised through shifts arranged so that more than one relay of workers does the same kind of work at the same time.

sub_structure.2: (2) The appropriate Government or (with approval) the Chief Inspector-cum-Facilitator may exempt establishments from this rule by written order, except that this exemption never applies to mines.

plain_english_summary: Employers generally can't double up overlapping shift crews doing the same job simultaneously, though exemptions are possible for non-mine establishments with government approval.

chapter_title: HOURS OF WORK AND ANNUAL LEAVE WITH WAGES
title: Restriction on double employment in factory and mine
text: No worker shall be required or allowed to work in a mine or factory if they have already worked at another similar establishment within the preceding twelve hours, except in prescribed circumstances.
plain_english_summary: To prevent worker fatigue and unsafe conditions, mine and factory workers can't take on a second job at another similar workplace within a 12-hour window.

chapter_title: HOURS OF WORK AND ANNUAL LEAVE WITH WAGES
title: Notice of periods of work
text: (1) Every establishment must display and correctly maintain a notice showing, for every day, the periods during which workers may be required to work.

sub_structure.3: (3) Any change to the work-period system that requires updating this notice must be intimated to the Inspector-cum-Facilitator beforehand, and (barring prior sanction) cannot take effect until a week has passed since the last change.

plain_english_summary: Establishments must publicly post their daily work-hour schedule, and any change to that schedule needs advance notice to the labour authority and a one-week cooling-off period.

chapter_title: HOURS OF WORK AND ANNUAL LEAVE WITH WAGES
title: Annual leave with wages
text: (1) Every worker who has worked 180 days or more in a calendar year is entitled to paid annual leave: one day per 20 days worked generally (one day per 15 days for adolescents and underground mine workers).

sub_structure.1_vi: (vi) On discharge, dismissal, resignation, superannuation or death during the year, the worker (or heirs) is entitled to cash payment for accrued but unused leave, payable within two working days (or two months for superannuation/death).
sub_structure.1_vii: (vii) Unused leave carries forward to the next year up to a cap of 30 days, though leave that was applied for but wrongly refused can carry forward without limit.
sub_structure.1_viii: (viii) Workers may demand encashment of accumulated leave at the end of the calendar year, and must encash any leave balance exceeding the 30-day cap.
sub_structure.3: (3) These leave rules don't override any more favourable leave entitlement a mine worker has under another law, award or contract.

plain_english_summary: Workers who put in at least 180 days a year earn paid annual leave (roughly 1 day per 20 worked), can carry forward or cash out unused leave up to a 30-day cap, and are paid out for any unused leave when they leave the job.

chapter_title: MAINTENANCE OF REGISTERS, RECORDS AND RETURNS
title: Maintenance of registers, records and filing of returns
text: An employer shall maintain prescribed registers (electronic or physical) covering work performed, normal daily working hours, weekly rest days, wages paid, leave and overtime, dangerous occurrences, and employment of adolescents.

sub_structure.b: (b) display notices at the workplace in the prescribed manner and form.
sub_structure.c: (c) issue wage slips to workers, electronically or otherwise.
sub_structure.d: (d) file periodic returns electronically or otherwise to the Inspector-cum-Facilitator.

plain_english_summary: Employers must keep detailed digital or paper records of hours, wages, leave and incidents, post required notices, issue wage slips, and file periodic returns with the labour authority.

title: Appointment of Inspector-cum-Facilitators
text: (1) The appropriate Government may, by notification, appoint Inspector-cum-Facilitators to exercise powers under this Code within their notified jurisdiction. (3) The Government may lay down a web-based, randomised inspection scheme rather than relying on discretionary site visits.

sub_structure.5: (5) A Chief Inspector-cum-Facilitator may be appointed for a State, several States, or the whole country.
sub_structure.8: (8) No person with a direct or indirect interest in a workplace or its business may be appointed as, or continue as, an Inspector-cum-Facilitator.
sub_structure.11: (11) Every such officer is deemed a public servant under section 21 of the Indian Penal Code.

plain_english_summary: The Code replaces the old model of inspectors with 'Inspector-cum-Facilitators', assigned via a randomised, largely web-based inspection scheme designed to reduce discretion and potential harassment — inspectors with a personal stake in a business can't be appointed.

title: Powers of Inspector-cum-Facilitators
text: (1) An Inspector-cum-Facilitator may enter and inspect any workplace, examine machinery/articles, inquire into accidents, require production of documents, search and seize records relating to a suspected offence, take samples/photographs/videos, and issue show-cause notices on safety, health and welfare matters.

sub_structure.1_xi: (xi) may direct dismantling, testing, or seizure of an article/substance believed to endanger health or safety, without destroying it unless necessary.
sub_structure.1_xiii: (xiii) may prosecute, conduct, or defend proceedings under this Code before any court.
sub_structure.2: (2) A person required to produce documents/information is deemed legally bound to do so under sections 175/176 of the Indian Penal Code.
sub_structure.3: (3) Search and seizure follow the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 as if under a warrant.

plain_english_summary: Inspector-cum-Facilitators get broad investigative powers — entry, inspection, document seizure, sampling, photography — and can even prosecute cases themselves, with refusal to cooperate treated as a criminal offence.

title: Powers and duties of District Magistrate
text: The District Magistrate shall, within his local jurisdiction, exercise such powers and duties of an Inspector-cum-Facilitator in respect of mines as may be prescribed by the Central Government.
plain_english_summary: District Magistrates are given a backup role exercising Inspector-cum-Facilitator powers specifically over mines within their district.

title: Third party audit and certification
text: (1) The appropriate Government may formulate a scheme empanelling qualified experts for third-party audit and certification of start-up establishments or notified classes of establishments.

sub_structure.2_a: (2)(a) Empanelled experts are assigned audits in a randomised manner through a web-based scheme.
sub_structure.2_c: (2)(c) They submit their audit/certification report to both the employer and the Inspector-cum-Facilitator.

plain_english_summary: As a lighter-touch compliance route, especially for start-ups, government-empanelled private experts (assigned randomly online) can conduct safety audits and certifications instead of a government inspector.

title: Special powers of Inspector-cum-Facilitator in respect of factory, mines, dock work and building or other construction work
text: Inspector-cum-Facilitators have emergency stop-work powers: for factories, they can prohibit work in hazardous conditions (order valid 3 days, extendable, appealable to the High Court); for mines, they can issue remediation notices and prohibit unsafe employment; for dock work and construction sites, they can prohibit work at dangerous sites pending safety fixes.

sub_structure.1_A_d: (1)(A)(d) Workers displaced by a factory prohibition order are entitled to wages/benefits, and the occupier must provide alternative employment where possible.
sub_structure.1_B_e: (1)(B)(e) Miners barred from unsafe work under a prohibition order are entitled to full wages for the period, or alternative employment at the same wage.
sub_structure.3: (3) Orders relating to construction sites can be appealed within 15 days to the Chief Inspector-cum-Facilitator or Government, decided within 60 days, but must be complied with in the meantime.

plain_english_summary: When a workplace poses serious, imminent danger, inspectors can immediately halt work in that factory, mine, dock, or construction site — but affected workers must still be paid, and employers get a structured, time-bound right of appeal.

title: Secrecy of information by Chief Inspector-cum-Facilitator or Inspector-cum-Facilitator, etc.
text: (1) Information and records obtained during inspection are confidential and cannot be disclosed, except where necessary for health/safety/welfare, unless the disclosure falls under a listed exception (courts, Boards/Committees, the employer, the Employees' Compensation Commissioner, etc.).

sub_structure.3: (3) Notwithstanding the Right to Information Act, 2005, an inspector cannot disclose a complainant's identity without consent, nor reveal to the employer that an inspection follows a specific complaint.

plain_english_summary: Inspectors must keep business information confidential, and — importantly — they're barred from revealing who filed a safety complaint, protecting whistleblowing workers from retaliation.

title: Facilities to be afforded to Inspector-cum-Facilitator
text: Every employer shall afford the Chief Inspector-cum-Facilitator, every Inspector-cum-Facilitator, and any authorised person all reasonable facilities to carry out entry, inspection, survey, measurement, examination or inquiry under this Code.
plain_english_summary: Employers must actively cooperate with and facilitate inspections, not just passively allow them.

title: Powers of special officer to enter, measure, etc., in relation to mine
text: An authorised government officer may, after giving at least three days' notice to the mine manager, enter and survey, level or measure a mine or its output at any time, day or night; in an emergency, this can be authorised without prior notice.
plain_english_summary: Beyond regular inspectors, specially authorised officers can independently survey and measure mine output, mostly with three days' notice but immediately in emergencies.

title: Medical officer
text: (1) The appropriate Government may appoint qualified medical practitioners as medical officers for factories, mines, plantations, motor transport undertakings and other prescribed establishments; they must disclose any personal interest in the establishment before taking office.

sub_structure.2_a: (2)(a) Duty to examine and certify workers in dangerous occupations/processes in mines or factories.
sub_structure.2_c: (2)(c) Duty to examine and certify adolescents' fitness for employment in hazardous work.

plain_english_summary: Government-appointed medical officers are responsible for certifying that workers (especially in hazardous jobs) and adolescents are medically fit for the work assigned to them.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISION RELATING TO EMPLOYMENT OF WOMEN
title: Employment of women
text: Women shall be entitled to be employed in all establishments for all types of work, and may also be employed before 6 a.m. and beyond 7 p.m. with their consent, subject to prescribed safety, holiday and working-hour conditions.
plain_english_summary: The Code removes blanket restrictions on women's working hours and job types — women can work night shifts and any role, but only with their own consent and with employer-provided safety safeguards.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISION RELATING TO EMPLOYMENT OF WOMEN
title: Adequate safety of employment of women in dangerous operation
text: Where the appropriate Government considers employment of women dangerous to their health and safety in a hazardous process or operation, it may require the employer to provide adequate safeguards before employing women for that operation.
plain_english_summary: For genuinely hazardous jobs, the government can insist employers put proper safety measures in place before women are assigned to that work, rather than barring them from it outright.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: Applicability of this Part
text: (1) This Part applies to every establishment employing 50 or more contract labour (or a manpower supply contractor engaging 50 or more) on any day in the preceding twelve months.

sub_structure.2: (2) It does not apply to establishments where only intermittent or casual work is performed — work is not 'intermittent' if performed for more than 120 days in the preceding year, or more than 60 days for seasonal work.

plain_english_summary: The contract-labour rules only kick in once an establishment or labour contractor crosses a 50-worker threshold, and genuinely occasional/seasonal work under set day-limits is carved out.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: Appointment of designated authority
text: The appropriate Government may appoint Gazetted officers as the designated licensing authority under section 119, defining their jurisdiction and vesting them with powers to issue and revoke contractor licences electronically.
plain_english_summary: A specific government officer is designated to handle contractor licensing electronically within a defined jurisdiction.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: Licensing of contractors
text: (1) No contractor may supply or engage contract labour, or execute work through contract labour, without a licence from the designated authority, which specifies the permitted headcount and required security deposit.

sub_structure.2: (2) A contractor who doesn't meet the standard licence criteria may instead get a 'work specific licence' valid only for a particular work order.
sub_structure.3_a: (3)(a) Licences can carry conditions on hours of work, wage fixation, and essential amenities for contract labour.

plain_english_summary: Contractors can't operate without a government licence that caps how many contract workers they can supply and requires a security deposit — smaller/less-qualified contractors can still get a narrower, work-specific licence.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: Procedure for issue or renewal of licence
text: (1) Licence applications must be made electronically with details of contract labour numbers, nature of work, and inter-State migrant worker employment.

sub_structure.3: (3) A licence under section 47(1) is valid for five years for the specified headcount; increasing the headcount requires an application to amend the licence along with additional security deposit.

plain_english_summary: Contractor licences run for five years and are tied to a specific worker headcount — scaling up the workforce requires formally amending the licence and topping up the security deposit.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: No fees or commission or any cost to workers
text: The contractor shall not charge, directly or indirectly, in whole or in part, any fee or commission from contract labour.
plain_english_summary: Contractors are flatly barred from charging workers any fee or commission to get or keep a job — a common exploitative practice this shuts down.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: Information regarding work order to be given to the appropriate Government
text: (1) When a contractor receives a work order to supply or execute work through contract labour, they must intimate the designated licensing authority within the prescribed time.

sub_structure.2: (2) Failure to give this intimation can lead to suspension or cancellation of the contractor's licence, after a show-cause opportunity.

plain_english_summary: Contractors must proactively report new work orders to the licensing authority, and skipping this can cost them their licence.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: Revocation, suspension and amendment of licence
text: (1) If a licence was obtained by misrepresentation, or the holder has violated licence conditions or this Part, the licensing authority may revoke or suspend it after giving the contractor an opportunity to show cause.

sub_structure.2: (2) The licensing authority may also amend a granted licence, subject to prescribed rules.

plain_english_summary: Contractor licences can be pulled or amended for fraud or rule-breaking, but only after due process — the contractor gets a chance to respond first.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: Appeal
text: (1) Anyone aggrieved by an order under sections 47, 48 or 51 may appeal to the prescribed appellate authority within 30 days (extendable for sufficient cause).

sub_structure.2: (2) The appellate authority must decide the appeal within 30 days of it being filed.

plain_english_summary: Contractors denied, or stripped of, a licence get a fast, defined right of appeal — decided within a month.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: Liability of principal employer for welfare facilities
text: Welfare facilities specified under sections 23 and 24 must be provided by the principal employer of the establishment to the contract labour employed there.
plain_english_summary: Even though contract workers are hired via a contractor, it's the principal employer (the business using their labour) who must ensure they get the same basic welfare facilities as regular staff.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: Effect of employing contract labour from a non-licenced contractor
text: Where a principal employer engages contract labour through a contractor who is required to hold, but has not obtained, a licence, that employment is deemed to be in contravention of this Code.
plain_english_summary: Using an unlicensed contractor isn't just the contractor's problem — the principal employer is automatically in breach of the Code too.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: Responsibility for payment of wages
text: (1) The contractor is responsible for paying wages to contract labour within the prescribed time, via bank transfer or electronic mode, with the amount reported electronically to the principal employer.

sub_structure.3: (3) If the contractor fails to pay or underpays, the principal employer must pay the wages/shortfall directly and recover it from the contractor.
sub_structure.4: (4) If the contractor still doesn't pay, the Government can order payment from the contractor's security deposit.

plain_english_summary: Wage payment to contract workers has a built-in safety net: if the contractor doesn't pay, the principal employer must step in and pay directly, then recover the money from the contractor or their security deposit.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: Experience certificate
text: Every contractor shall, on demand, issue an experience certificate to contract labour detailing the work performed by them.
plain_english_summary: Contract workers can demand a formal record of the work they did, useful for future job applications.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: Prohibition of employment of contract labour in core activities
text: (1) Contract labour is generally prohibited in the 'core activities' of an establishment, except where such work is customarily contracted out, doesn't need full-time workers, or is needed to handle a sudden spike in workload.

sub_structure.2_a: (2)(a) The Government may appoint a designated authority to advise on whether a given activity counts as a 'core activity'.
sub_structure.2_b: (2)(b) A party who disputes a core-activity classification can apply to the appropriate Government for a decision.

plain_english_summary: Businesses generally can't outsource their core business functions to contract labour — only peripheral, occasional, or workload-spike-driven work — though there's a formal process to dispute what counts as 'core'.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: Power to exempt in special cases
text: In an emergency, the appropriate Government may, by notification, exempt any establishment, class of establishments, or class of contractors from all or any provisions of this Code, subject to specified conditions and for a specified period.
plain_english_summary: The government keeps an emergency escape valve to temporarily suspend contract-labour rules for specific businesses if circumstances demand it.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: Applicability of Part II
text: This Part applies to every establishment in which ten or more inter-State migrant workers are employed or were employed on any day of the preceding twelve months.
plain_english_summary: Special protections for inter-State migrant workers kick in once an establishment has employed ten or more of them at any point in the past year.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: Facilities to inter-State migrant workers
text: Every contractor/employer of an establishment employing inter-State migrant workers must ensure suitable working conditions given the worker is away from their home State, report fatal accidents/serious injuries to authorities in both States and to the worker's next of kin, and extend all benefits (ESI, EPF, medical check-ups) available to other workers.
plain_english_summary: Migrant workers must get the same benefits (provident fund, health insurance, health check-ups) as local workers, plus extra safeguards recognising they're far from home, including cross-State accident reporting.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: Journey allowance
text: The employer shall pay every inter-State migrant worker a lump sum annual amount for a to-and-fro journey between their native place and place of employment, per prescribed eligibility, frequency and travel class rules.
plain_english_summary: Migrant workers get a paid annual trip home, funded by the employer.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: Benefits of public distribution system, etc.
text: The appropriate Government shall create schemes allowing inter-State migrant workers to access public distribution system (ration) benefits in either their native or destination State, and enabling portability of building-worker cess-fund benefits to the destination State.
plain_english_summary: Migrant workers shouldn't lose access to subsidised rations or construction-worker welfare fund benefits just because they've crossed a State border — these are made portable.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: Toll free helpline
text: The appropriate Government may provide a toll-free helpline facility for inter-State migrant workers in the prescribed manner.
plain_english_summary: A dedicated helpline can be set up so migrant workers have a direct channel to reach out for help.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: Study of inter-State migrant workers
text: The appropriate Government may provide for study of inter-State migrant workers in the prescribed manner.
plain_english_summary: The government can commission research studies specifically tracking migrant worker conditions and trends.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: Past liabilities
text: No suit or proceeding can be brought to recover any unsettled debt owed by an inter-State migrant worker to a contractor or principal employer after completion of the worker's employment; such debt is deemed extinguished once employment ends.
plain_english_summary: Once a migrant worker's job ends, any money they still owed the contractor or employer (e.g. advances) is legally wiped out — protecting workers from being trapped by debt bondage.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: Prohibition of employment of audio-visual worker without agreement
text: (1) No person shall be employed as an audio-visual worker unless a written agreement is entered into (by the producer, or the producer with a contractor, or the contractor) and registered with the competent authority.

sub_structure.2_c: (2)(c) Where the worker is engaged through a contractor, the agreement must make the producer also liable (with a right to reimbursement) if the contractor fails to pay wages or meet other obligations.
sub_structure.4: (4) The agreement must cover assignment nature, wages/PF benefits, health, safety, hours, welfare, and a dispute-resolution mechanism, with unresolved disputes escalating to the Industrial Tribunal as an industrial dispute; wages must be paid electronically.

plain_english_summary: Film/TV/audio-visual workers must have a registered written contract before they can be hired at all, and the producer stays on the hook for the worker's pay even if a middleman contractor fails to deliver.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: Managers
text: (1) Every mine shall be under a sole qualified manager, appointed by the owner/agent (who may appoint themselves if qualified). (2) The manager is responsible for overall management, control, supervision and direction of the mine.

sub_structure.3: (3) Except in an emergency, the owner/agent cannot bypass the manager to give instructions directly to mine staff on statutory matters.

plain_english_summary: Every mine needs one accountable, qualified manager in charge day-to-day, and owners generally can't go around the manager to give safety-related instructions directly to workers.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: Code not to apply in certain cases
text: (1) Most of the Code (except sections 35, 38, 40, 41 and 44) doesn't apply to prospecting-only excavations, or mines extracting low-risk materials like kankar, sand, clay, building stone, etc., subject to prescribed conditions.

sub_structure.3: (3) If the exempting conditions cease to be met, the full Code becomes immediately applicable, and the employer must report this change to the authority.

plain_english_summary: Small-scale prospecting digs and quarries for common, low-hazard materials get a lighter compliance load — but only as long as they keep meeting the specific exemption conditions.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: Power of manager to act in emergency
text: (1) In an emergency (serious risk, accident, act of God, or urgent equipment breakdown work), a mine manager may permit work that would otherwise contravene the hours-of-work and rest-day rules, strictly to protect the mine's or workers' safety.

sub_structure.2: (2) Every such emergency action must be recorded with the circumstances and reported to the Chief Inspector-cum-Facilitator or Inspector-cum-Facilitator.

plain_english_summary: Mine managers can override normal working-hour limits in a genuine emergency to protect lives or the mine itself, but every such override must be documented and reported to the safety authorities.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: Employment of persons below eighteen years of age
text: (1) No person below 18 may work in any mine. (2) Apprentices/trainees aged 16 or above may work under supervision, with trainees (other than apprentices) needing prior Inspector-cum-Facilitator approval.

sub_structure.3: (3) The Central Government may prescribe medical examination requirements to confirm fitness and enforce the age limits for apprentices, trainees, and employees.

plain_english_summary: Mine work is off-limits to anyone under 18, with a narrow, supervised exception for 16+ apprentices and approved trainees.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: Exemption to certain persons
text: The Central Government may make rules exempting certain persons or categories of mine employees from the working-hours, weekly-holiday, double-employment and work-notice provisions (sections 25(1), 26(1), 30 and 31(1)).
plain_english_summary: Certain categories of mine staff (e.g. supervisory roles) can be carved out from standard hours-of-work rules by Central Government rule.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: Establishment, maintenance of rescue services and vocational training
text: The Central Government may prescribe vocational training and rescue and recovery services for persons employed in a mine.
plain_english_summary: Mines are expected to have organised rescue capability and skills training for their workforce, per Central Government rules.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: Decision of question whether a mine is covered under this Code
text: If a question arises whether an excavation, working, or premises adjacent to a mine (where mineral/coke processing occurs) counts as part of the mine under this Code, the Central Government decides, and a certificate signed by a Secretary in the Ministry of Labour and Employment is conclusive proof.
plain_english_summary: Disputes about whether a particular site legally counts as 'part of a mine' are settled conclusively by the Central Government, not the courts.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: Licence to industrial premises and person
text: (1) No employer may use any premises as an 'industrial premises' for beedi/cigar making without a valid licence, obtained by application specifying the maximum workers to be employed and a premises plan.

sub_structure.4: (4) In deciding whether to grant a licence, the authority considers the premises' suitability, the applicant's experience/financial resources, whether the application is bona fide (not benami), and local labour welfare interests.
sub_structure.5: (5) A licence is valid for five years and renewable.
sub_structure.7: (7) The licence can be cancelled or suspended for misrepresentation, fraud, or contravention of the Part, after a hearing.

plain_english_summary: Anyone running a beedi- or cigar-making workshop needs a five-year renewable licence, and the government screens applicants for genuine ownership (no shell/benami fronts), financial capacity, and worker welfare track record before granting it.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: Appeals
text: Anyone aggrieved by a refusal to grant/renew, or a cancellation/suspension, of a beedi/cigar industrial premises licence may appeal to the appellate authority under section 119(6), which can confirm, modify, or reverse the decision.
plain_english_summary: Beedi/cigar business owners denied a licence have a formal appeal route.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: Permission to work by employees outside industrial premises
text: (1) The State Government may permit wetting/cutting of beedi tobacco leaves outside the industrial premises, on the employer's application, subject to prescribed conditions, with records maintained.

sub_structure.3: (3) Generally, beedi/cigar manufacturing must happen inside licensed premises — except workers given raw material to make beedi/cigar at home.

plain_english_summary: Beedi work usually has to happen at the licensed workshop, though narrow exceptions allow certain steps (or full home-based piecework) outside it under specific permission.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: Part not to apply to self-employed persons in private dwelling houses
text: This Part doesn't apply to an owner/occupier of a private dwelling who manufactures beedi/cigar with the help of family members living with and dependent on them (excluding children as defined under child labour law).
plain_english_summary: A small family-run, home-based beedi operation using only family labour (no children) is exempt from this Part's licensing regime entirely.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: Prohibition of employment of certain persons in certain building or other construction work
text: No person known or believed by the employer to be deaf, have defective vision, or have a tendency to giddiness shall be required or allowed to work on building/construction operations likely to risk accident to themselves or others.
plain_english_summary: Construction employers must keep workers with certain physical conditions (that create real accident risk, like poor vision or giddiness) away from specifically hazardous tasks like working at height.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: Approval, licensing and registration of factories
text: (1) The appropriate Government may make rules on submission/certification of factory plans, prior site permission for construction/extension, and licensing/renewal (with fees).

sub_structure.2: (2) If no order is communicated within 30 days of an electronic application for site/construction permission, the permission is deemed granted.
sub_structure.3: (3) A refusal can be appealed within 30 days — to the Central Government if the State Government refused, or to the State Government otherwise.

plain_english_summary: Setting up or expanding a factory needs government sign-off on site and plans, but there's a built-in 'deemed approval' if the government doesn't respond within 30 days, plus an appeal route if refused.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: Liability of owner of premises in certain circumstances
text: Where premises/buildings are leased to different occupiers as separate factories sharing common facilities (fire safety, hygiene, ventilation, canteens, restrooms, creches), the premises owner and all occupiers using those facilities are jointly and severally responsible for maintaining them.
plain_english_summary: In shared industrial buildings with multiple factory tenants, everyone using the common safety and welfare facilities is jointly on the hook for keeping them properly maintained — no one tenant can free-ride.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: Power to apply Code to certain premises
text: (1) The appropriate Government may, by notification, declare the factory provisions applicable to any place where a manufacturing process is (or is ordinarily) carried on, regardless of worker count. (2) Once so declared, it's deemed a factory, the owner deemed the occupier, and workers there deemed workers under the Code.
plain_english_summary: The government can pull small manufacturing operations under full factory-safety regulation by simple notification, even if they'd otherwise fall below the usual worker-count threshold for being a 'factory'.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: Dangerous operations
text: The appropriate Government may make rules for factories with processes exposing workers to serious injury/poisoning/disease risk: declaring the process dangerous, restricting employment of pregnant women in it, requiring periodic employer-funded medical exams, and mandating welfare/protective equipment.
plain_english_summary: For genuinely dangerous manufacturing processes, the government can impose extra protections — including restricting pregnant women's exposure and mandating regular, employer-paid medical checks.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: Constitution of site appraisal committee
text: (1) The appropriate Government may constitute site appraisal committees to recommend on applications for locating or expanding a factory involving a hazardous process.

sub_structure.2: (2) The committee must give its recommendation within 30 days of receiving the application.

plain_english_summary: Before a hazardous factory can be sited or expanded, an expert committee reviews and recommends on the application within a fixed 30-day window.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: Compulsory disclosure of information by occupier
text: (1) Occupiers of hazardous-process factories must disclose all hazard/health-risk information to workers, the Inspector-cum-Facilitator, the local authority, and the nearby public. (2) They must lay down a health and safety policy at registration and update authorities on changes.

sub_structure.4: (4) Occupiers must draw up (with Chief Inspector approval) an on-site emergency plan and disaster-control measures, publicised to workers and nearby residents.
sub_structure.6: (6) Failing to notify the Chief Inspector before starting a new hazardous process can lead to the factory's licence being cancelled, on top of any penalty.

plain_english_summary: Hazardous factories can't keep their risks secret — they must proactively disclose dangers and emergency plans to workers, regulators, and the surrounding community, or risk losing their operating licence.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: Specific responsibility of the occupier in relation to hazardous processes
text: Every occupier of a hazardous-process factory must maintain accessible, up-to-date health/medical records for exposed workers, appoint qualified people to competently supervise hazardous-substance handling, and arrange medical exams before, during (every 12 months), and after a worker's assignment to hazardous work.
plain_english_summary: Workers exposed to hazardous substances get a documented, ongoing medical monitoring trail — before they start the risky job, annually while doing it, and after they stop.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: National Board to inquire into certain situations
text: (1) In an extraordinary situation at a hazardous-process factory, the Central Government may direct the National Board to inquire into the health/safety standards followed, to find the causes of failure and prevent recurrence.

sub_structure.2: (2) The National Board's recommendations are advisory only.

plain_english_summary: After a serious incident at a hazardous factory, the National Safety Board can be tasked with a root-cause inquiry, though its findings are advisory rather than binding.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: Emergency standards
text: (1) Where no safety standards exist (or existing ones are inadequate) for a hazardous process, the Central Government may direct the Directorate General Occupational Safety and Health (or an authorised institution) to lay down emergency standards.

sub_structure.2: (2) These emergency standards are enforceable immediately, with the same effect as formal rules, until formally incorporated into the rules.

plain_english_summary: If a safety gap is discovered for a hazardous process, the government doesn't have to wait for the full rule-making process — it can issue emergency standards that are immediately enforceable.
keywords: Directorate General Occupational Safety and Health

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: Permissible limits of exposure of chemicals and toxic substances
text: The maximum permissible exposure limits for chemical and toxic substances in a factory's manufacturing process shall be as prescribed by the State Government.
plain_english_summary: Chemical/toxic exposure in factories is capped at State-government-set safety thresholds, not left to employer discretion.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: Right of workers to warn about imminent danger
text: (1) Workers in a hazardous-process factory who reasonably apprehend imminent danger to life/health may notify the person in-charge (directly or via the Safety Committee) and simultaneously notify the Inspector-cum-Facilitator.

sub_structure.2: (2) The person in-charge must take immediate remedial action if satisfied of the danger, and report the action to the Inspector-cum-Facilitator.
sub_structure.3: (3) If not satisfied, they must still refer the matter to the Inspector-cum-Facilitator, whose decision is final.

plain_english_summary: Workers in hazardous factories have a direct, dual-track channel to flag imminent danger — to management and the regulator at the same time — and management can't just dismiss the concern without an independent check.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: Appeal against the order of Inspector-cum-Facilitator in case of factory
text: The appropriate Government may prescribe the manner and appellate authority to whom a factory manager/occupier may appeal against an Inspector-cum-Facilitator's order, and the procedure for disposing of such appeals.
plain_english_summary: Factory occupiers get a defined appeal mechanism against inspector orders, per government-prescribed procedure.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: Power to make rules to exempt
text: (1) The appropriate Government may make rules defining supervisory/managerial/confidential-position employees who are exempt from this Code's provisions, and may prescribe conditional exemptions for other workers/establishments.

sub_structure.2: (2) The Government or Chief Inspector-cum-Facilitator may, by written order, exempt some or all adult workers in an establishment from specified provisions, subject to conditions.

plain_english_summary: Senior/confidential-role employees can be carved out of certain worker protections, and the government retains general flexibility to grant conditional exemptions to adult workers.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: Facilities for workers in plantation
text: (1) The State Government may require every plantation employer to provide housing (with drinking water, kitchen, toilet) for workers and families, creche facilities where 50+ workers are employed, educational facilities where 25+ children aged 6-12 are present, health facilities (or ESI coverage), and recreational facilities.

sub_structure.2: (2) The employer must fund/maintain these welfare facilities from their own resources or via Central/State/local government schemes.

plain_english_summary: Plantation workers and their families get a comprehensive welfare package — housing, creches, schooling access, healthcare and recreation — funded by the employer, government schemes, or a mix.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR CONTRACT LABOUR AND INTER-STATE MIGRANT WORKER, ETC.
title: Safety
text: (1) Plantation employers must arrange for worker safety in using, handling, storing and transporting insecticides, pesticides and toxic chemicals. (3) Employers must appoint qualified supervisors for this. (4) Workers handling such chemicals must be trained on hazards and emergency response.

sub_structure.5: (5) Exposed workers must be medically examined periodically, and (6) health records maintained and accessible to them.
sub_structure.7: (7) Employers must provide washing/bathing facilities and protective clothing/equipment.
sub_structure.8: (8) Permissible chemical concentration limits must be displayed on-site, along with hazard warning notices.

plain_english_summary: Plantation workers who handle pesticides and chemicals get a full protective package — training, protective gear, regular medical checks, health records, and visible on-site hazard information.

title: General penalty for offences
text: Except where otherwise expressly provided, any contravention of this Code, its rules, regulations, bye-laws, standards, or written orders makes the employer/principal employer liable to a penalty of Rs. 2 lakh to Rs. 3 lakh, plus a further penalty of up to Rs. 2,000 per day for continuing contravention after conviction.
plain_english_summary: This is the Code's default penalty clause: most violations without a specific penalty elsewhere carry a fine between Rs. 2–3 lakh, with daily fines added for ongoing non-compliance.

title: Punishment for causing obstruction to Chief Inspector-cum-Facilitator or Inspector-cum-Facilitator, etc.
text: (1) Willfully obstructing an Inspector-cum-Facilitator (or authorised officer/expert) from their duties, refusing them entry, refusing to produce required documents, or failing to comply with a lawful order is punishable with up to 3 months' imprisonment, or a fine up to Rs. 1 lakh, or both.

sub_structure.2: (2) A repeat conviction for the same offence carries up to 6 months' imprisonment, or a fine of Rs. 1–2 lakh, or both.

plain_english_summary: Obstructing safety inspectors — blocking entry, hiding documents, ignoring orders — is a criminal offence, with harsher penalties for repeat offenders.

title: Penalty for non-maintenance of register, records and non-filing of returns, etc.
text: (1) Failing to maintain registers/documents/returns, or failing to produce a required register/plan/record/report, attracts a penalty of Rs. 50,000 to Rs. 1 lakh.

sub_structure.2: (2) A repeat conviction raises the penalty range to Rs. 50,000 up to Rs. 2 lakh.

plain_english_summary: Basic recordkeeping failures (missing registers, unfiled returns) carry a fixed monetary penalty, doubling in ceiling for repeat offences.

title: Penalty for contravention of provisions relating to employment of women, contract labour, etc.
text: (1) Contravening the Code or any order restricting/regulating employment of women, audio-visual workers, contract labour, or persons below 18 in mines attracts a penalty of Rs. 50,000 to Rs. 1 lakh.

sub_structure.2: (2) A repeat offence is punishable with up to 3 months' imprisonment, or a fine up to Rs. 2 lakh, or both.

plain_english_summary: Violating employment restrictions meant to protect vulnerable worker groups (women, migrants, minors in mines) escalates from a fine to potential imprisonment on repeat offence.

title: Punishment for falsification of records, etc.
text: (1) Producing false records, counterfeit documents, false statements, falsified plans, or knowingly false returns/reports/notices under this Code is punishable with up to 3 months' imprisonment, or a fine up to Rs. 1 lakh, or both.

sub_structure.2: (2) A repeat conviction carries up to 6 months' imprisonment, or a fine of Rs. 1–2 lakh, or both.

plain_english_summary: Faking compliance documents — fabricated plans, false statements, forged reports — is a criminal offence with escalating punishment for repeat falsification.

title: Penalty for omission to furnish plans, etc.
text: Anyone who, without reasonable excuse (burden of proof on them), fails to submit a required plan, return, notice, register, record or report in the prescribed form, manner or time, is liable to a penalty of Rs. 1–2 lakh.
plain_english_summary: Missing required paperwork deadlines carries a substantial fine, and it's on the accused to prove they had a reasonable excuse, not on the government to disprove one.

title: Punishment for disclosure of information
text: (1) A Chief Inspector-cum-Facilitator, Inspector-cum-Facilitator, or other covered person who discloses confidential information (under sections 39/121) without government consent is punishable with up to 3 months' imprisonment, or a fine up to Rs. 1 lakh, or both.

sub_structure.2: (2) No court can try this offence without prior sanction of the appropriate Government.

plain_english_summary: Inspectors who leak confidential business information face criminal liability themselves — the confidentiality duty cuts both ways.

title: Punishment for wrongfully disclosing results of analysis
text: Anyone who publishes or discloses the results of an analysis of a sample of a substance used under this Code (other than for a prosecution) is punishable with up to 6 months' imprisonment, or a fine up to Rs. 50,000, or both.
plain_english_summary: Lab analysis results of workplace substances can't be publicly disclosed except for legitimate prosecution purposes — protecting proprietary/technical information from misuse.

title: Punishment for contravention of provisions of duties relating to hazardous processes
text: (1) Failing key employer duties (under section 6(1)(a)-(h)/6(2), section 13(d), or section 80) relating to hazardous processes is punishable with up to 2 years' imprisonment and a fine up to Rs. 5 lakh, plus up to Rs. 25,000/day for continuing contravention post-conviction.

sub_structure.2: (2) If the contravention continues beyond one year after conviction, the punishment escalates to up to 3 years' imprisonment or a fine of Rs. 20 lakh, or both.

plain_english_summary: Ignoring core safety duties around hazardous processes is treated seriously — up to 2 years in prison and steep daily fines for ongoing non-compliance, escalating further for long-term defiance.

title: Punishment for contravention of provisions of duties relating to safety provisions resulting in an accident
text: (1) Where non-compliance with safety duties results in an accident causing death, the offender faces up to 2 years' imprisonment or a fine of at least Rs. 5 lakh, or both; if it causes serious bodily injury, up to 1 year imprisonment or a fine of Rs. 2–4 lakh, or both, with at least 50% of the fine directed as victim/family compensation.

sub_structure.2: (2) A repeat conviction doubles the punishment.

plain_english_summary: When a safety violation actually causes a death or serious injury, the penalties become substantially harsher, and courts must direct at least half the fine to the victim or their family as compensation.

title: Special provision for contravention of order under section 38
text: Continuing to work in contravention of a stop-work order issued under section 38 is punishable with up to 2 years' imprisonment and a fine up to Rs. 5 lakh; a fine below Rs. 2 lakh requires the court to record specific reasons.
plain_english_summary: Defying an inspector's emergency stop-work order is treated as a serious offence, with a built-in minimum fine unless the court explains why it's going lower.

title: Failure to appoint manager in mine
text: Failing to appoint a qualified mine manager under section 67 is punishable with up to 3 months' imprisonment, or a fine up to Rs. 1 lakh, or both.
plain_english_summary: Running a mine without a legally required qualified manager is itself a punishable offence.

title: Offences by employees
text: (1) An employee who contravenes duties imposed on them under this Code (other than the section 13(d) duty) is liable to a penalty of up to Rs. 10,000.

sub_structure.2: (2) The employer isn't automatically guilty just because an employee is convicted — only if the employer failed to take all reasonable preventive measures.

plain_english_summary: Employees can personally be fined for breaking safety rules, but this doesn't automatically implicate the employer unless the employer also dropped the ball on prevention.

title: Prosecution of owner, agent or manager of mine
text: No prosecution against a mine owner, agent or manager can be launched except by the Chief Inspector-cum-Facilitator, District Magistrate, or an authorised Inspector-cum-Facilitator, who must first be satisfied that due diligence to prevent the offence was lacking.

sub_structure.proviso2: For offences in the course of technical direction/management of a mine, the District Magistrate needs the Chief Inspector-cum-Facilitator's prior approval before prosecuting.

plain_english_summary: Prosecuting mine leadership isn't automatic — it requires sign-off from a senior safety official who first checks whether due diligence was genuinely lacking.

title: Exemption of owner, agent or manager of mine or occupier of factory from liability in certain cases
text: A charged owner/agent/manager/occupier can, with proper notice, bring the actual alleged offender before the court; if they prove due diligence or that the other person acted without their knowledge/consent, that other person is convicted instead and they are discharged.
plain_english_summary: Mine or factory leadership can shift criminal liability to the actual wrongdoer (e.g. a rogue supervisor) if they can prove they exercised due diligence and had no hand in the offence.

title: Offences by companies, etc.
text: (1) Where a company commits an offence, every person in charge of and responsible for its business at the time, as well as the company, is deemed guilty — unless they prove the offence occurred without their knowledge or despite due diligence.

sub_structure.2: (2) If the offence is shown to be due to a director/manager/company secretary/officer's consent, connivance, or neglect, that individual is also deemed guilty personally.

plain_english_summary: Corporate offences reach individual executives and directors personally, not just the corporate entity — unless they can show they exercised proper due diligence.

title: Limitation of prosecution and cognizance of offences
text: (1) Before prosecuting most offences, the Inspector-cum-Facilitator must give the employer 30 days to comply, and drop prosecution if they do — except for accidents or repeat violations of the same kind within 3 years.

sub_structure.2: (2) Courts can't take cognizance of an offence unless a complaint is filed within 6 months of the Inspector-cum-Facilitator learning of it.
sub_structure.3: (3) Only a Metropolitan Magistrate or Judicial Magistrate First Class (or higher) can try offences under this Code.

plain_english_summary: The Code favours a 'comply-first' approach — employers generally get a 30-day cure period before facing prosecution, except for accidents or repeat offenders, and there's a strict 6-month complaint deadline.

title: Power of officers of appropriate Government to impose penalty in certain cases
text: (1) For penalties under specified sections (12(3), 94, 96, 97, 99, 106, 114(3)), the Government may appoint an Under Secretary-rank officer (or equivalent) to hold an inquiry and impose the penalty, with summons/document-production powers.

sub_structure.3: (3) An aggrieved person may appeal to a Deputy Secretary-rank appellate authority within 60 days.
sub_structure.5: (5) Failure to pay an imposed penalty within 90 days is itself punishable with a fine of Rs. 25,000 to Rs. 2 lakh.

plain_english_summary: Certain routine penalties are handled administratively by a government officer rather than a court — faster than criminal prosecution, but with a right of appeal and a penalty for non-payment.

title: Jurisdiction of court for entertaining proceedings, etc., for offence
text: For deciding which court has jurisdiction over an offence connected to an establishment, the place where the establishment is currently situated is deemed to be the place where the offence was committed.
plain_english_summary: Prosecutions are anchored to the establishment's current location, simplifying where a case can be filed.

title: Power of court to make orders
text: (1) On convicting a mine/factory/dock employer, the court may additionally order them to remedy the violation within a specified (extendable) period, suspending further liability for the continuing offence during that period.

sub_structure.2: (2) If the remedial order isn't fully complied with by the deadline, the employer commits a further offence punishable with up to 6 months' imprisonment or a fine of Rs. 100/day of non-compliance, or both.

plain_english_summary: Courts can order convicted employers to actually fix the underlying problem, with a grace period — but blowing that deadline triggers fresh criminal liability.

title: Power to compound offences
text: (1) Many listed penalties/offences (e.g. under sections 12(3), 94, 96, 97, 99, 106, 100, 101, 103(1)(b), 105) can be compounded (settled) by a notified government officer — for a penalty, at 50% of the maximum; for an offence, at 75% of the maximum fine.

sub_structure.2: (2) Compounding discharges the person from further proceedings on that matter.
sub_structure.5: (5) Compounding is unavailable for a repeat offence/penalty within 3 years of an earlier compounding or conviction for the same thing.

plain_english_summary: Many offences can be settled by paying a set percentage of the maximum fine instead of going through full prosecution — a faster route, but it's closed off to repeat offenders within a 3-year window.

title: Social security fund
text: (1) The appropriate Government shall establish a social security fund for unorganised workers' welfare, credited with amounts from compounded offences (section 114(4)) and penalties (section 111(6)).

sub_structure.3: (3) The fund is administered for unorganised workers' welfare, including transferring amounts to funds under other unorganised-worker welfare laws.

plain_english_summary: Fines and settlement amounts collected under this Code get recycled into a dedicated welfare fund for unorganised (informal-sector) workers, rather than just going to general government revenue.

title: Delegation of powers
text: The Central Government may, by notification, direct that any power exercisable by it under this Code may also be exercised by a State Government or a subordinate officer/authority, subject to specified conditions.
plain_english_summary: The Centre can delegate its powers under this Code down to State Governments or specific officials, allowing for more localised administration.

title: Onus as to age
text: (1) In an age-related offence, if the court prima facie believes a person is under the relevant age, the burden shifts to the accused to prove otherwise.

sub_structure.2: (2) Age is verified in order of preference: Aadhaar card, then school/matriculation birth certificate, then municipal/Panchayat birth certificate, and only failing all these, an ossification test or other medical age test.

plain_english_summary: In disputes over whether a worker was underage, the accused employer bears the burden of proof, and age is determined through a defined hierarchy of documents, with medical testing as a last resort.

title: Onus of proving limits of what is practicable, etc.
text: In proceedings alleging failure to comply with a duty to do something, the accused bears the burden of proving it was not reasonably practicable, or that all practicable measures were taken to comply.
plain_english_summary: When an employer is accused of not meeting a safety duty, it's up to them to prove they did everything reasonably possible — not for the prosecution to prove they didn't.

title: Common licence for contractor, factories and to industrial premises, etc.
text: (1) A person can apply electronically for a single common licence covering a factory, beedi/cigar premises, and contract-labour engagement (or any combination), from a Government-designated authority.

sub_structure.4: (4) The licence must be issued within 45 days, or is automatically deemed issued if the authority fails to act; the authority is accountable for such failure, and any rejection must state reasons.
sub_structure.5: (5) Licences already validly held under prior Central labour laws are deemed valid under this Code until their existing expiry.

plain_english_summary: The Code consolidates what used to be multiple separate licences (factory, beedi/cigar premises, contract labour) into one common application process, with an automatic 'deemed granted' safeguard if the government sits on the application past 45 days.

title: Effect of law and agreements inconsistent with Code
text: (1) This Code overrides any inconsistent law, award, agreement or contract of service — except that an employee keeps any more favourable benefit they were already entitled to under such an award/agreement.

sub_structure.2: (2) Employers and employees may still voluntarily agree to more favourable rights/privileges than the Code provides.

plain_english_summary: This Code sets the floor, not the ceiling — it overrides less favourable terms elsewhere, but any existing or future agreement that's more generous to the worker still stands.

title: Power of appropriate Government to direct inquiry in certain cases
text: (1) After a serious/epidemic-level accident or occupational disease, the Government may appoint assessors with legal/special knowledge to inquire into causes, fix responsibility and recommend prevention measures.

sub_structure.2: (2) The Government may also direct a survey into workplace safety/health conditions or the health impact of a work activity.
sub_structure.3: (3) The inquiry officer/committee has civil-court powers to summon witnesses and compel document production.

plain_english_summary: For major incidents or disease outbreaks tied to work, the government can commission an independent, legally empowered inquiry — with real teeth to compel testimony and evidence — to find causes and prevent recurrence.

title: Publication of reports
text: The appropriate Government may, if it thinks fit, publish any report (or extracts) submitted to it by the National Board or a State Advisory Board.
plain_english_summary: Safety board reports can be made public at the government's discretion, supporting transparency.

title: Powers of Central Government to give directions
text: The Central Government may give directions to a State Government for implementing the provisions of this Code.
plain_english_summary: The Centre retains oversight authority to direct States on how they implement this Code.

title: General restriction on disclosure of information
text: (1) No person shall disclose confidential manufacturing/business/process information learned in the course of official duties. (2) Exceptions apply for disclosure with the owner's written consent, or for legal/arbitration/criminal proceedings under the Code.
plain_english_summary: Officials handling confidential business information are barred from leaking it, except with consent or for genuine legal proceedings.

title: Jurisdiction of civil courts barred
text: No civil court shall have jurisdiction over any matter covered by this Code, and no civil court may grant an injunction against anything done or intended under this Code.
plain_english_summary: Disputes covered by this Code must go through the Code's own dispute mechanisms, not civil courts — and civil courts can't block government/employer actions taken under it.

title: Protection of action taken in good faith
text: (1) No legal proceeding lies against any person for anything done in good faith under this Code, its rules, regulations, bye-laws or orders. (2) The same protection extends to the Government, Boards/Committees, and their members/officers/authorised persons for damage caused by good-faith action.
plain_english_summary: Officials and regulators acting honestly and in good faith under this Code — even if it later causes some harm — are shielded from lawsuits, so long as they weren't acting in bad faith or negligently.

title: Power to exempt in special cases
text: (1) The appropriate Government may, by notification and subject to conditions/time limits, exempt any establishment or class of establishments from all or any provisions of this Code.

sub_structure.2: (2) A State Government may specifically exempt new factories from all/any provisions for a specified period from the start of commercial production, in the public interest of boosting economic activity and employment; pre-existing Factories Act exemption notifications remain valid for their remaining term.

plain_english_summary: The government has broad, discretionary power to grant temporary compliance holidays to businesses — including a specific carve-out to attract new factories by exempting them from parts of the Code for a set startup period.

title: Power to exempt during public emergency
text: In a public emergency, disaster or pandemic (nationwide or regional), the appropriate Government may, by notification, exempt any workplace or work activity from all or any Code provisions for up to one year at a time, subject to conditions.
plain_english_summary: During emergencies like a pandemic, the government can temporarily suspend parts of this Code for affected workplaces, capped at a one-year exemption window per notification.

title: Power to exempt public institution
text: The appropriate Government may exempt a workshop/workplace attached to a public educational, training, research or information institution from all or any Code provisions, though exemptions from hours-of-work and holiday rules require the institution to submit an approved scheme no less favourable than the Code.
plain_english_summary: Workshops attached to schools, research labs, or training institutes get flexibility from ordinary factory-style rules, but can't shortchange people on working hours and holidays without an approved, equally protective alternative scheme.

title: Persons required to give notice, etc., legally bound to do so
text: Every person required to give notice or furnish information to an authority under this Code is legally bound to do so within the meaning of section 176 of the Indian Penal Code.
plain_english_summary: Reporting obligations under this Code carry the same legal weight as any statutory reporting duty under the Indian Penal Code — ignoring them is itself an offence.

title: Power of Central Government to amend Schedule
text: The Central Government may, by notification, amend any Schedule to this Code by addition, alteration or omission, and the Schedule is deemed amended accordingly upon notification.
plain_english_summary: The technical Schedules (hazardous processes, safety standards, notifiable diseases) can be updated by the Central Government through notification, without needing a full legislative amendment.

title: Power to remove difficulties
text: (1) If any difficulty arises in implementing the Code, the Central Government may, by Gazette order, make provisions (not inconsistent with the Code) to remove the difficulty, but only within 2 years of the Code coming into force.

sub_structure.2: (2) Every such order must be laid before both Houses of Parliament.

plain_english_summary: A standard transitional safety valve: the government gets a two-year window to iron out practical implementation kinks by order, subject to Parliamentary oversight.

title: Power of appropriate Government to make rules
text: (1) The appropriate Government may make rules (after prior publication) for carrying out the Code's purposes. (2) These cover an extensive list of matters delegated throughout the Code — application forms and fees, registration and licensing procedures, Safety Committee composition, notice formats for accidents/diseases, overtime limits, and dozens of other prescribed details referenced in specific sections.
plain_english_summary: This is the Code's master rule-making clause: nearly every 'as may be prescribed' reference throughout the Act traces back here, letting the appropriate (Central or State) Government fill in the operational details via subordinate rules.

title: Power of Central Government to make rules on specified matters
text: (1) The Central Government may make rules (after prior publication) for its own specifically delegated matters under the Code.
